title: Ranibizumab for neovascular age-related macular degeneration
text: MARINA randomised people with minimally classic or occult choroidal neovascularisation due to AMD to monthly intravitreal ranibizumab 0.3 mg or 0.5 mg or sham injection for 24 months. About 95 percent of ranibizumab treated eyes lost fewer than 15 letters at 12 months compared with about 62 percent of sham treated eyes, and mean acuity improved with ranibizumab while it declined with sham.

title: Ranibizumab versus verteporfin for neovascular age-related macular degeneration
text: ANCHOR compared monthly ranibizumab with verteporfin photodynamic therapy in predominantly classic choroidal neovascularisation due to AMD. Ranibizumab was superior: a much larger proportion of ranibizumab treated eyes avoided a loss of 15 letters at one year, and on average acuity improved with ranibizumab and fell with photodynamic therapy.

title: Intravitreal aflibercept (VEGF trap-eye) in wet age-related macular degeneration
text: The VIEW 1 and VIEW 2 trials compared intravitreal aflibercept, including 2 mg every 8 weeks after three monthly loading doses, with monthly ranibizumab 0.5 mg in neovascular AMD. At week 52 every aflibercept regimen was non inferior to monthly ranibizumab for maintaining vision, so aflibercept every 8 weeks achieved similar outcomes with fewer injections.

title: Efficacy, durability, and safety of intravitreal faricimab up to every 16 weeks for neovascular age-related macular degeneration (TENAYA and LUCERNE)
text: TENAYA and LUCERNE were two phase 3 randomised, double masked trials comparing faricimab given at intervals of up to every 16 weeks with aflibercept every 8 weeks in neovascular AMD. Faricimab was non inferior to aflibercept for change in best corrected acuity at one year, and nearly half of faricimab treated eyes were on a 16 week interval at week 48.

title: Efficacy, durability, and safety of intravitreal faricimab with extended dosing up to every 16 weeks in diabetic macular oedema (YOSEMITE and RHINE)
text: YOSEMITE and RHINE were two phase 3 randomised, double masked trials in diabetic macular oedema comparing faricimab every 8 weeks and faricimab with a personalised treatment interval of up to every 16 weeks against aflibercept every 8 weeks. Both faricimab regimens were non inferior to aflibercept for acuity gain at one year, and more than half of eyes in the personalised arm reached a 16 week interval.

title: Ranibizumab for diabetic macular edema: results from 2 phase III randomized trials: RISE and RIDE
text: RISE and RIDE randomised people with diabetic macular oedema to monthly intravitreal ranibizumab 0.3 mg or 0.5 mg or sham injection. Significantly more ranibizumab treated eyes gained 15 or more letters at 24 months, retinal thickness fell rapidly, and ranibizumab also reduced the risk of retinopathy progression.

title: Intravitreal aflibercept for diabetic macular edema (VIVID and VISTA)
text: VIVID and VISTA compared intravitreal aflibercept 2 mg every 4 weeks, and every 8 weeks after five monthly doses, with macular laser photocoagulation in diabetic macular oedema. Both aflibercept regimens were superior to laser for change in best corrected acuity at week 52.

title: Aflibercept, bevacizumab, or ranibizumab for diabetic macular edema (DRCR Retina Network Protocol T)
text: Protocol T randomised eyes with centre involving diabetic macular oedema to aflibercept, bevacizumab or ranibizumab. All three improved vision. When baseline acuity was mildly reduced (20/32 to 20/40) the differences between drugs were small, but when baseline acuity was 20/50 or worse aflibercept produced a greater improvement at one year.

title: Panretinal photocoagulation vs intravitreous ranibizumab for proliferative diabetic retinopathy (DRCR Retina Network Protocol S)
text: Protocol S compared intravitreal ranibizumab with panretinal photocoagulation for proliferative diabetic retinopathy. At two years ranibizumab was non inferior for visual acuity, with less peripheral visual field loss, fewer vitrectomies and less development of diabetic macular oedema, although it required repeated injections and follow up.

title: Selective laser trabeculoplasty versus eye drops for first-line treatment of ocular hypertension and glaucoma (LiGHT)
text: The LiGHT trial randomised people with newly diagnosed, untreated open angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension in the UK to selective laser trabeculoplasty first or eye drops first and followed them for 36 months. Quality of life was similar between groups, SLT first was cost effective, and around three quarters of eyes in the SLT group were at target pressure without drops at three years.

title: Latanoprost for open-angle glaucoma (UKGTS): a randomised, multicentre, placebo-controlled trial
text: The United Kingdom Glaucoma Treatment Study randomised people with newly diagnosed open angle glaucoma to latanoprost or placebo eye drops. Latanoprost significantly reduced the risk of visual field deterioration within 24 months, the first placebo controlled demonstration that pressure lowering drops preserve the visual field in open angle glaucoma.

title: Reduction of intraocular pressure and glaucoma progression: results from the Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial
text: The Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial randomised people with newly detected open angle glaucoma to laser trabeculoplasty with betaxolol or to no immediate treatment. Progression occurred in 45 percent of treated and 62 percent of untreated participants, and each 1 mmHg of pressure reduction was associated with roughly a 10 percent lower risk of progression.

title: The Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study: a randomized trial determines that topical ocular hypotensive medication delays or prevents the onset of primary open-angle glaucoma
text: The Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study randomised people with ocular hypertension to topical pressure lowering medication or observation. Treatment reduced the five year incidence of primary open angle glaucoma from 9.5 percent to 4.4 percent. Thinner central corneal thickness was among the baseline factors associated with conversion to glaucoma.
